question_text: A Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) is best defined as a wireless communication network that:
options: Uses radio network equipment carried on airborne or spaceborne vehicles
Relies exclusively on ground-based cell towers and fibre
Connects two mobile handsets without any base station
Operates only at optical wavelengths between ground stations
correct_answer: Uses radio network equipment carried on airborne or spaceborne vehicles

question_text: Terrestrial networks (TN) and non-terrestrial networks (NTN) differ primarily in their:
options: Infrastructure and coverage areas
Choice of programming language for the core network
Use of the TCP/IP protocol suite
Billing and subscription models
correct_answer: Infrastructure and coverage areas

question_text: In NTN terminology, a 'spaceborne' platform refers to:
options: Drones and balloons flying in the lower atmosphere
Fibre-optic backbone links between data centres
Satellite communication using artificial satellites orbiting the Earth
Ground gateways that steer antennas toward satellites
correct_answer: Satellite communication using artificial satellites orbiting the Earth

question_text: Which of the following are examples of airborne NTN platforms?
options: GEO, MEO and LEO satellites
Fixed gNBs and fibre cables
Undersea cables and microwave relay towers
Drones (UAVs) and High-Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS)
correct_answer: Drones (UAVs) and High-Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS)

question_text: The airborne NTN platform abbreviated HAPS stands for:
options: High-Availability Packet Switch
High-Altitude Platform Station
Hybrid Aerial Positioning System
High-Altitude Payload Satellite
correct_answer: High-Altitude Platform Station

question_text: One motivation for NTN cited in the 6G vision is that terrestrial networks currently:
options: Cover less than 40% of the Earth's surface
Cover more than 95% of the Earth's surface
Are completely immune to natural disasters
Provide uniform, seamless coverage over the oceans
correct_answer: Cover less than 40% of the Earth's surface

question_text: An NTN platform creating large beams to illuminate remote farms, oceans and IoT devices anywhere on Earth illustrates which NTN use-case category?
options: Service continuity
Service scalability
Service ubiquity
Service localization
correct_answer: Service ubiquity

question_text: A cellular subscriber who boards a cruise ship or an aircraft and would otherwise lose coverage is best served by which NTN use-case category?
options: Service ubiquity
Service scalability
Service redundancy
Service continuity
correct_answer: Service continuity

question_text: Broadcasting the same content, such as a software update or a live event, to many users over a large area with one wide NTN beam illustrates:
options: Service scalability
Service continuity
Service ubiquity
Service isolation
correct_answer: Service scalability

question_text: Deploying terrestrial base stations across sparsely populated deserts, mountains and oceans is generally avoided mainly because:
options: Radio waves cannot physically travel over open water
Spectrum is legally unavailable outside cities
Satellites legally prohibit ground towers in those areas
It is not cost-effective and often lacks a viable business case
correct_answer: It is not cost-effective and often lacks a viable business case

question_text: A major driver of the decades-long success of terrestrial mobile networks has been:
options: The complete absence of regulation in the sector
International standardization ensuring vendor compatibility and lower costs
Exclusive reliance on proprietary, closed hardware
The use of a single global operator worldwide
correct_answer: International standardization ensuring vendor compatibility and lower costs

question_text: Historically, the satellite communications market has been fragmented largely because of:
options: Excessive standardization that stifled all innovation
Government bans on manufacturing satellites
An unlimited supply of cheap, interchangeable devices
A lack of standardization, making interoperability between vendors difficult
correct_answer: A lack of standardization, making interoperability between vendors difficult

question_text: Compared with satellite systems, a key characteristic of terrestrial networks is that they offer:
options: Global coverage of oceans and polar regions
Low propagation delay, which is important for real-time applications
Complete immunity to congestion and interference
Very high latency measured in hundreds of milliseconds
correct_answer: Low propagation delay, which is important for real-time applications

question_text: The infrastructure of a terrestrial network is characterised by:
options: Satellites, HAPS and drones operating in the sky
Only end-user handsets communicating peer-to-peer
Fixed ground-based base stations (e.g., gNodeB), cables and switching centres
Optical inter-satellite links operating in orbit
correct_answer: Fixed ground-based base stations (e.g., gNodeB), cables and switching centres

question_text: The current relationship between the satellite and terrestrial mobile communication industries is best described as:
options: Progressively converging toward TN-NTN integration
Diverging into two fully separate ecosystems
Remaining two permanently isolated industrial chains
Being replaced entirely by wired networks
correct_answer: Progressively converging toward TN-NTN integration

question_text: The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) is significant to NTN because it:
options: Manufactures and launches communication satellites
Completed the first global 5G NR standard and is extending it to support satellites
Owns and operates the Starlink constellation
Issues spectrum licences to operators in each country
correct_answer: Completed the first global 5G NR standard and is extending it to support satellites

question_text: In 5G rollout, NTN is expected to serve unserved areas such as isolated regions, aircraft and vessels, and additionally to serve:
options: Underserved areas such as sub-urban/rural regions, upgrading limited terrestrial performance
Only dense urban centres that already have 5G
Only areas that already have a fibre backhaul
Only military installations, never civilian users
correct_answer: Underserved areas such as sub-urban/rural regions, upgrading limited terrestrial performance

question_text: Generally, compared with NTN, terrestrial networks are described as providing:
options: Lower reliability and higher bit error rates
Identical reliability under all conditions
Higher reliability and lower bit error rates
Reliable service only over the open oceans
correct_answer: Higher reliability and lower bit error rates

question_text: A frequently cited advantage of NTN over TN during earthquakes, floods or armed conflict is that NTN:
options: Can maintain coverage when terrestrial infrastructure is damaged or destroyed
Is completely unaffected by weather of any kind
Requires no ground gateways whatsoever
Eliminates the need for any radio spectrum
correct_answer: Can maintain coverage when terrestrial infrastructure is damaged or destroyed

question_text: The integration of satellite communications into 5G is anticipated to facilitate:
options: Anything, anytime, anywhere connectivity
Connectivity only within licensed urban cells
Fixed-line-only broadband services
Connectivity that works solely during daylight hours
correct_answer: Anything, anytime, anywhere connectivity

question_text: Which statement best summarises the primary limitations of terrestrial networks?
options: Unlimited reach but uniformly very high latency
Restricted global reach, vulnerability to physical damage, and high cost in rugged terrain
Perfect disaster resilience but poor data speed
Global ocean coverage but no urban coverage
correct_answer: Restricted global reach, vulnerability to physical damage, and high cost in rugged terrain

question_text: The TE 456 course explicitly shifts its focus from:
options: Legacy satellite communication toward Non-Terrestrial Networks
Non-Terrestrial Networks back toward fixed telephony
5G NR back toward 2G GSM systems
Optical fibre toward copper access networks
correct_answer: Legacy satellite communication toward Non-Terrestrial Networks

question_text: Relative to extensive terrestrial deployments in remote regions, NTNs are described as:
options: Always more expensive, with no coverage benefit
Equivalent in cost but lower in coverage
Potentially more cost-effective, while extending coverage and providing a backup
Cheaper only because they need no spectrum
correct_answer: Potentially more cost-effective, while extending coverage and providing a backup

question_text: In the Ghanaian context discussed, rural regions have largely lagged in 4G coverage, leaving many users dependent on:
options: 5G standalone networks
Satellite broadband that is already deployed
Fibre-to-the-home connections
3G networks
correct_answer: 3G networks

question_text: An NTN is characterised as a network that uses a communications platform at an altitude of:
options: A few hundred metres, like a typical cell tower
Exactly at sea level
Below the tropopause only
More than tens of kilometres above the Earth
correct_answer: More than tens of kilometres above the Earth

question_text: According to Kepler's laws as applied to satellites, satellite orbits are:
options: Perfect circles centred exactly on the Earth's core
Straight lines tangent to the equator
Squares traced around the two poles
Ellipses with the Earth at one of the foci
correct_answer: Ellipses with the Earth at one of the foci

question_text: As a satellite's orbital altitude decreases and it gets closer to Earth, its:
options: Orbital speed decreases and its period lengthens
Orbital speed increases and its orbital period reduces
Speed and period both remain constant
Field of view increases while its speed drops
correct_answer: Orbital speed increases and its orbital period reduces

question_text: A geostationary (GEO) satellite orbits at an altitude of approximately:
options: 550 km

question_text: A GEO satellite appears stationary to a fixed observer on Earth because it:
options: Does not actually move at all in its orbit
Completes one orbit in about 24 hours, matching the Earth's rotation
Orbits the Earth in under 90 minutes
Is physically held in place by a tether
correct_answer: Completes one orbit in about 24 hours, matching the Earth's rotation

question_text: Theoretically, near-global coverage (excluding the extreme poles) can be achieved with how many GEO satellites?
options: One
Twelve
Twenty-four
Three
correct_answer: Three

question_text: Because of its high altitude, a GEO satellite exhibits a round-trip propagation delay on the order of:
options: About 1 ms
About 600 ms
About 25 ms
About 50 microseconds
correct_answer: About 600 ms

question_text: A recognised disadvantage of GEO satellites is:
options: The need for constant satellite-to-satellite handovers
An extremely short, negligible propagation delay
A requirement for thousands of satellites for coverage
Poor signal coverage at the extreme polar regions
correct_answer: Poor signal coverage at the extreme polar regions

question_text: Non-Geostationary Earth Orbit (NGEO) satellites are characterised by:
options: Fixed positions above the equator at all times
Orbital periods of exactly 24 hours
Orbital periods of less than 24 hours and positions that change relative to observers
Being permanently invisible from the ground
correct_answer: Orbital periods of less than 24 hours and positions that change relative to observers

question_text: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites typically operate at altitudes of:
options: Exactly 35,786 km
Above 100,000 km

question_text: A typical LEO satellite has an orbital period of about:
options: 24 hours
6 to 12 hours
90 minutes
One week
correct_answer: 90 minutes

question_text: Because of their low altitude, LEO satellites offer a small one-way propagation delay on the order of:
options: About 600 ms
About 83 ms
Several seconds
1 to 5 ms
correct_answer: 1 to 5 ms

question_text: Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) satellites orbit at altitudes ranging from about:
options: 35,786 km, fixed
Below 300 km

question_text: MEO satellites are described as the backbone of global navigation; for example, GPS uses at least:
options: 24 MEO satellites
3 GEO satellites
Thousands of LEO satellites
A single HAPS platform
correct_answer: 24 MEO satellites

question_text: Achieving continuous global coverage with LEO satellites requires:
options: A single satellite
Hundreds of satellites, forming a mega-constellation
Exactly three satellites
No more than six satellites
correct_answer: Hundreds of satellites, forming a mega-constellation

question_text: Starlink provides broadband using thousands of LEO satellites flying at about 550 km, achieving a round-trip delay of roughly:
options: 600 ms
250 ms
25 ms
2 ms
correct_answer: 25 ms

question_text: A disadvantage of NGEO (LEO/MEO) systems compared with GEO is that they:
options: Have far higher latency than GEO satellites
Require dynamic hand-offs and active ground-antenna tracking of moving satellites
Cannot provide any coverage of polar regions
Need only a stationary dish with no tracking
correct_answer: Require dynamic hand-offs and active ground-antenna tracking of moving satellites

question_text: For High-Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS), 3GPP focuses on altitudes between:
options: 8 and 50 km
1 and 5 km
correct_answer: 8 and 50 km

question_text: Because a HAPS maintains its position relative to the Earth's surface, it:
options: Uses only Earth-moving beams like a fast LEO satellite
Has a round-trip delay of about 600 ms
Uses Earth-fixed beams like a GEO satellite, with delay comparable to terrestrial networks
Covers a smaller area than a single terrestrial gNB
correct_answer: Uses Earth-fixed beams like a GEO satellite, with delay comparable to terrestrial networks

question_text: Compared with spaceborne NTN, airborne NTN platforms:
options: Have a much larger propagation delay than GEO
Are completely immune to strong winds and storms
Provide permanent global coverage from a single unit
Deploy quickly at lower cost with smaller delay, but face stabilization and weather challenges
correct_answer: Deploy quickly at lower cost with smaller delay, but face stabilization and weather challenges

question_text: The satellite-period relation Period = C x distance^1.5 indicates that the orbital period:
options: Is independent of the orbital distance
Decreases as the orbital distance increases
Increases with the 1.5 power of the orbital distance
Varies linearly with the orbital distance
correct_answer: Increases with the 1.5 power of the orbital distance

question_text: The three types of beams used in an NTN to provide radio coverage are Earth-fixed, Earth-moving, and:
options: Polar-locked beams
Quasi-Earth-fixed beams
Counter-rotating beams
Ground-anchored beams
correct_answer: Quasi-Earth-fixed beams

question_text: An Earth-fixed beam is one that:
options: Sweeps across a new area at every instant
Covers the same fixed geographic region on Earth at all times
Covers area X then abruptly jumps to area Y
Can only be produced by a LEO satellite
correct_answer: Covers the same fixed geographic region on Earth at all times

question_text: An Earth-moving beam is characterised by the fact that it:
options: Always illuminates the exact same area permanently
Covers a slightly different geographic area at each successive instant as the platform moves
Is produced only by stationary GEO satellites
Requires beam steering to remain fixed on one spot
correct_answer: Covers a slightly different geographic area at each successive instant as the platform moves

question_text: With a quasi-Earth-fixed beam covering area X from t1 to t2 and then a different area, continuity over area X is maintained because:
options: The satellite physically stops moving in its orbit
One beam covers all geographic areas simultaneously
The user device switches to a wired connection
An incoming quasi-Earth-fixed beam replaces the outgoing beam over the same area
correct_answer: An incoming quasi-Earth-fixed beam replaces the outgoing beam over the same area

question_text: GEO satellites, with beam footprints from roughly 200 to 3,500 km, are most commonly used for services such as:
options: Ultra-low-latency competitive online gaming
Sub-millisecond industrial control loops
Short-range indoor positioning
Weather monitoring, TV broadcasting, and remote sensing/positioning
correct_answer: Weather monitoring, TV broadcasting, and remote sensing/positioning

question_text: In 5G NR-NTN, the 'service link' is:
options: The connection between the satellite and the gateway
The direct link between two satellites in orbit
The 5G radio access (Uu interface) between the UE and the satellite
The wired link between the gateway and the 5GC
correct_answer: The 5G radio access (Uu interface) between the UE and the satellite

question_text: The 'feeder link' (satellite radio interface, SRI) describes the connection between:
options: The UE and the satellite
The gNB and the 5G core network
The satellite and the ground gateway
Two user devices directly
correct_answer: The satellite and the ground gateway

question_text: In NTN, the term SAN refers to the:
options: Satellite Access Node
Secure Access Network
Satellite Antenna Numerology
Signal Attenuation Node
correct_answer: Satellite Access Node

question_text: A transparent (bent-pipe) NTN payload:
options: Amplifies, filters and frequency-translates the signal without onboard baseband processing
Fully decodes and re-encodes the signal in orbit
Hosts the complete gNB onboard the satellite
Terminates the Uu interface on the satellite
correct_answer: Amplifies, filters and frequency-translates the signal without onboard baseband processing

question_text: With a transparent payload, the NTN gNB is located:
options: Onboard the satellite itself
Inside the UE handset
Distributed across several satellites
On the ground, typically co-located with the gateway
correct_answer: On the ground, typically co-located with the gateway

question_text: In the transparent-payload architecture, the 5G Uu radio interface terminates at:
options: The satellite payload
The terrestrial gNB, not at the satellite
The UE only
The 5G core network
correct_answer: The terrestrial gNB, not at the satellite

question_text: A regenerative (decode-and-forward) payload differs from a transparent one in that it:
options: Only amplifies and forwards, with no onboard processing
Removes the need for any gateway or 5G core
Incorporates gNB functions onboard, terminating the Uu interface at the satellite
Cannot support inter-satellite links
correct_answer: Incorporates gNB functions onboard, terminating the Uu interface at the satellite

question_text: A key latency advantage of the regenerative architecture is that:
options: The satellite hardware becomes far simpler and cheaper
It eliminates the need for a service link entirely
The single-way latency includes only the service link, reducing round-trip time
The Uu interface terminates on the ground
correct_answer: The single-way latency includes only the service link, reducing round-trip time

question_text: An Inter-Satellite Link (ISL) in a regenerative NTN:
options: Connects a satellite to a terrestrial fibre ring
Connects NTN payloads to one another, allowing relay toward a distant gateway
Links a UE directly to the 5G core network
Replaces the feeder link with a wired cable
correct_answer: Connects NTN payloads to one another, allowing relay toward a distant gateway

question_text: A disaggregated gNB is split into a:
options: Uplink Unit and a Downlink Unit
Service Unit and a Feeder Unit
Primary Unit and a Secondary Unit
Centralized Unit (CU) and a Distributed Unit (DU)
correct_answer: Centralized Unit (CU) and a Distributed Unit (DU)

question_text: When a regenerative payload hosts only the gNB-DU while the CU stays on the ground, the feeder link carries the:
options: F1 interface (F1-C signalling and F1-U user-plane traffic)
Uu air interface only
N6 interface toward the Internet
ISL optical control channel
correct_answer: F1 interface (F1-C signalling and F1-U user-plane traffic)

question_text: In a multi-connectivity NTN scenario, the NTN UE:
options: Connects to exactly one satellite at any time
Uses only a wired backhaul connection
Cannot connect to any terrestrial network
Simultaneously communicates with multiple radio or core networks
correct_answer: Simultaneously communicates with multiple radio or core networks

question_text: For direct NTN access to handheld UEs within FR1, the commonly used frequency bands are:
options: Only the mmWave FR2 bands
Only optical/visible-light bands
S-band and L-band
Only sub-100 MHz HF bands
correct_answer: S-band and L-band

question_text: The first 5G NR-NTN specifications target enhanced Mobile Broadband via 5G NR and machine-type communication via:
options: Bluetooth Low Energy
NB-IoT
Wi-Fi 6
LoRaWAN
correct_answer: NB-IoT

question_text: The most challenging NTN characteristic inhibiting low-latency communication is:
options: The small physical size of satellite antennas
The long round-trip time due to the large UE-to-satellite distance
The absence of any modulation scheme
The low cost of ground gateways
correct_answer: The long round-trip time due to the large UE-to-satellite distance

question_text: Typical one-way latency values quoted for NTN range from about 30-40 ms in LEO up to:
options: About 5 ms in GEO constellations
About 1 ms in GEO constellations
About 544 ms in GEO constellations
About 60 ms in GEO constellations
correct_answer: About 544 ms in GEO constellations

question_text: The Doppler (carrier-frequency) shift in NTN arises mainly because:
options: The satellite is perfectly stationary in space
The satellite, and possibly the UE, moves, causing a time-variant carrier-frequency deviation
The gateway periodically changes its IP address
The UE increases its transmit power over time
correct_answer: The satellite, and possibly the UE, moves, causing a time-variant carrier-frequency deviation

question_text: The 'Doppler rate' in an NTN specifically refers to:
options: The fixed frequency offset at a single instant
The variation of the Doppler shift over the connection time
The data rate carried on the feeder link
The rate at which satellites are launched
correct_answer: The variation of the Doppler shift over the connection time

question_text: To compensate the uplink Doppler shift, the UE typically:
options: Estimates its position via GNSS and uses satellite ephemeris to pre-adjust its uplink carrier frequency
Randomly hops across all available subcarriers
Increases transmit power to overpower the shift
Waits until the satellite stops moving
correct_answer: Estimates its position via GNSS and uses satellite ephemeris to pre-adjust its uplink carrier frequency

question_text: Ionospheric propagation that causes a rotation of the waveform's polarization is known as:
options: Doppler rotation
Keplerian precession
Rayleigh fading
Faraday rotation
correct_answer: Faraday rotation

question_text: Beyond round-trip time and Doppler effects, a further NTN technical challenge affecting the PHY/MAC layers is:
options: Moving cells caused by satellite motion
Perfectly static, unchanging coverage areas
The complete absence of any base station
An unlimited supply of available spectrum
correct_answer: Moving cells caused by satellite motion

question_text: In the transparent-payload protocol stack, the termination points for RRC, PDCP, RLC, MAC and PHY are on the:
options: Satellite payload and the gateway
NTN UE and the NTN gNB, since the satellite and gateway are transparent
5G core network and the Internet
UE and the satellite only
correct_answer: NTN UE and the NTN gNB, since the satellite and gateway are transparent

question_text: When a regenerative payload houses the full gNB, the RRC terminates in the satellite, which results in:
options: A much longer RRC reaction time than the transparent case
No RRC layer being needed at all
RRC termination out on the Internet
A shorter reaction time for RRC procedures
correct_answer: A shorter reaction time for RRC procedures

question_text: In NTN, the gateway is the terrestrial station that:
options: Acts as the end-user handset
Generates the satellite's onboard electrical power
Connects the gNB (or 5GC) functions to the satellite
Provides GNSS positioning directly to the UE
correct_answer: Connects the gNB (or 5GC) functions to the satellite

question_text: The regenerative payload's on-board processor (OBP), inserted between the LNA and the HPA, enables:
options: Only analogue amplification with no processing
Elimination of the downlink antenna
Error correction and routing of packets between beams before retransmission
A direct wired connection to the 5G core
correct_answer: Error correction and routing of packets between beams before retransmission

question_text: At its most basic, a communication satellite acts as a:
options: Passive mirror that reflects signals unchanged
Data-storage warehouse held in orbit
Repeater - a receiver linked to a transmitter using different frequencies
GNSS timing clock and nothing more
correct_answer: Repeater - a receiver linked to a transmitter using different frequencies

question_text: A satellite communication system is divided into two main segments:
options: The uplink segment and the billing segment
The analogue segment and the digital segment
The civilian segment and the military segment
The space segment and the earth/ground segment
correct_answer: The space segment and the earth/ground segment

question_text: The communications payload of a satellite consists of two distinct parts:
options: Solar panels and batteries
Thrusters and fuel tanks
Ground gateways and user terminals
Repeaters/transponders and antennas
correct_answer: Repeaters/transponders and antennas

question_text: A transponder changes the uplink carrier frequency to a different downlink frequency. In the Ku band this is, for example, from:
options: 14 GHz on the uplink to 11 GHz on the downlink
11 GHz on the uplink to 14 GHz on the downlink
20 GHz on the uplink to 30 GHz on the downlink
14 GHz on the uplink to 14 GHz on the downlink
correct_answer: 14 GHz on the uplink to 11 GHz on the downlink

question_text: If a payload bandwidth of 500 MHz is divided into channels of 36 MHz each, the approximate number of transponders is:
options: About 12
About 500
About 36
About 2
correct_answer: About 12

question_text: A satellite repeater always uses different frequencies for receive and transmit mainly in order to:
options: Avoid interference between the incoming and outgoing signals
Save electrical power onboard the satellite
Comply with Kepler's laws of motion
Reduce the satellite to a single antenna
correct_answer: Avoid interference between the incoming and outgoing signals

question_text: A transparent (bent-pipe) repeater typically consists of a low-noise amplifier, a high-power amplifier, and:
options: A mixer with a local oscillator for frequency conversion
An on-board baseband processor for decoding
A GNSS receiver for satellite positioning
A propulsion thruster for station-keeping
correct_answer: A mixer with a local oscillator for frequency conversion

question_text: Unlike a transparent repeater, a regenerative (processing) repeater:
options: Simply amplifies and forwards everything, including noise
Demodulates the uplink to baseband, corrects errors, then remodulates for the downlink
Cannot change the carrier frequency at all
Contains no amplifiers of any kind
correct_answer: Demodulates the uplink to baseband, corrects errors, then remodulates for the downlink

question_text: A benefit of a regenerative repeater over a bent-pipe one is that it:
options: Consumes far less power and mass
Operates without any antennas
Works only with analogue signals
Cleans the signal by decoding and correcting errors instead of forwarding noise
correct_answer: Cleans the signal by decoding and correcting errors instead of forwarding noise

question_text: Which of the following is a space-platform (bus) subsystem that supports the payload?
options: Physical Downlink Shared Channel (PDSCH)
User Plane Function (UPF)
Resource Block scheduler
Attitude and Orbit Control System (AOCS)
correct_answer: Attitude and Orbit Control System (AOCS)

question_text: The Telemetry, Tracking, and Command (TTC&M) subsystem is responsible for:
options: Amplifying and retransmitting the user carriers
Allocating IP addresses to the user devices
Monitoring subsystem health, tracking position, and executing commands from ground control
Performing OFDMA resource scheduling
correct_answer: Monitoring subsystem health, tracking position, and executing commands from ground control

question_text: The three main satellite links are the service link, the feeder link, and the:
options: Inter-satellite link (ISL)
Fibre backhaul link
Ethernet control link
Terrestrial microwave link
correct_answer: Inter-satellite link (ISL)

question_text: Inter-satellite links (ISLs) can be implemented using:
options: Either radio-frequency or optical links
Only copper cabling
Only acoustic signalling
Only undersea fibre
correct_answer: Either radio-frequency or optical links

question_text: The performance of transmitting equipment is measured by its EIRP, which is:
options: The ratio of antenna gain to system noise temperature
The Boltzmann constant multiplied by temperature
The power fed to the antenna multiplied by the antenna gain in the considered direction
The received carrier-to-noise density ratio
correct_answer: The power fed to the antenna multiplied by the antenna gain in the considered direction

question_text: The receiver figure of merit, G/T, is the ratio of:
options: The transmit power to the antenna gain
The antenna receive gain to the system noise temperature
The carrier power to the user bit rate
The uplink frequency to the downlink frequency
correct_answer: The antenna receive gain to the system noise temperature

question_text: A satellite link budget is fundamentally used to:
options: Predict whether the received signal will be strong enough relative to the noise
Schedule the satellite's launch window
Allocate telephone numbers to users
Determine the satellite's orbital inclination
correct_answer: Predict whether the received signal will be strong enough relative to the noise

question_text: Noise power spectral density N0 is defined as:
options: The antenna gain divided by the temperature
The EIRP minus the free-space path loss
The product of the Boltzmann constant k and the system noise temperature T
The carrier power multiplied by the bit rate
correct_answer: The product of the Boltzmann constant k and the system noise temperature T

question_text: Which of the following is a link (propagation) loss accounted for in a satellite link budget?
options: The Boltzmann constant of the receiver
The EIRP of the transmitter
The number of transponders onboard
Free-space path loss together with rain/atmospheric attenuation
correct_answer: Free-space path loss together with rain/atmospheric attenuation

question_text: In 5G NR, Frequency Range 1 (FR1) spans approximately:
options: 410 MHz to 7.125 GHz
24 to 52 GHz
50 to 66 GHz
Below 100 MHz only
correct_answer: 410 MHz to 7.125 GHz

question_text: In 5G NR, a resource block (RB) in the frequency domain is defined as:
options: 14 consecutive subcarriers
10 consecutive subframes
A single OFDM symbol
12 consecutive subcarriers
correct_answer: 12 consecutive subcarriers

question_text: A 5G NR radio frame lasts 10 ms and contains:
options: One subframe of 10 ms
Ten subframes of 1 ms each
Fourteen subframes of 1 ms each
Twelve subframes of 0.5 ms each
correct_answer: Ten subframes of 1 ms each

question_text: In 5G NR, the subcarrier spacing given by delta-f = 2^u x 15 kHz means that it:
options: Is fixed at 15 kHz for every deployment
Decreases as the numerology u increases
Scales flexibly with the numerology u (e.g., 15, 30, 60, 120 kHz)
Depends only on the carrier frequency band
correct_answer: Scales flexibly with the numerology u (e.g., 15, 30, 60, 120 kHz)

question_text: Which set lists three 5G NR downlink physical channels?
options: PUSCH, PRACH and PUCCH
AMF, SMF and UPF
PDSCH, PDCCH and PBCH
RRC, PDCP and RLC
correct_answer: PDSCH, PDCCH and PBCH

question_text: In the 5G initial access procedure, the UE first performs cell search using:
options: The random-access preamble on PRACH
The RRC Connection Setup message
The synchronization signals PSS and SSS
The Sounding Reference Signal (SRS)
correct_answer: The synchronization signals PSS and SSS

question_text: To increase spectral efficiency, the 5G NR physical layer adopts which channel-coding techniques?
options: Convolutional and Reed-Solomon coding only
Turbo coding, exactly as used in LTE, only
No channel coding at all
Polar coding and LDPC coding
correct_answer: Polar coding and LDPC coding
